questions.q: State the formula for the velocity of the centre of mass of a system of n particles and give its SI unit.
questions.a: \( \vec{V}_{cm} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n m_i \vec{v}_i}{M} \), SI unit: m/s. A wrong answer (e.g., omitting the denominator M or using scalar addition) reveals the student has not grasped that centre-of-mass velocity is a mass-weighted average, not a simple arithmetic mean.

questions.q: A child sits at one end of a long trolley moving uniformly on a smooth horizontal floor. The child gets up and runs about on the trolley. What happens to the speed of the centre of mass of the (trolley + child) system? Explain why.
questions.a: The speed of the centre of mass remains unchanged (equal to the initial trolley speed V). The forces between child and trolley are internal; no external horizontal force acts, so \( \vec{F}_{ext} = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{A}_{cm} = 0 \). A student who says the speed changes confuses internal motion with centre-of-mass motion and ignores that frictionless floor implies zero external horizontal force.

questions.q: Two particles of masses 2 kg and 3 kg move along the x-axis with velocities \( 4 \hat{i} \) m/s and \( -2 \hat{i} \) m/s respectively. Calculate the velocity of their centre of mass.
questions.a:
Given: \( m_1 = 2 \) kg, \( \vec{v}_1 = 4 \hat{i} \) m/s; \( m_2 = 3 \) kg, \( \vec{v}_2 = -2 \hat{i} \) m/s. Total mass \( M = 5 \) kg.
\( \vec{V}_{cm} = \frac{2 \times 4 \hat{i} + 3 \times (-2 \hat{i})}{5} = \frac{8 \hat{i} - 6 \hat{i}}{5} = \frac{2 \hat{i}}{5} = 0.4 \hat{i} \) m/s.
Unit check: (kg·m/s)/kg = m/s ✓. A wrong sign or arithmetic error shows the student cannot handle vector addition with signs or mass-weighting.

questions.q: A projectile of mass 5 kg is fired at 60° with speed 100 m/s. At the highest point it explodes into two fragments of masses 2 kg and 3 kg. The 2 kg fragment comes to rest immediately after explosion. Find the velocity of the 3 kg fragment just after explosion. (Take g = 10 m/s², ignore air resistance.)
questions.a:
At highest point, projectile velocity is purely horizontal: \( v_x = 100 \cos 60° = 50 \) m/s.
Initial momentum: \( \vec{p}_i = 5 \times 50 \hat{i} = 250 \hat{i} \) kg·m/s.
After explosion: 2 kg fragment has \( \vec{v}_1 = 0 \), 3 kg fragment has \( \vec{v}_2 \).
Conservation of momentum (no external horizontal force): \( 250 \hat{i} = 2 \times 0 + 3 \vec{v}_2 \Rightarrow \vec{v}_2 = \frac{250}{3} \hat{i} \approx 83.3 \hat{i} \) m/s.
A student who uses energy conservation or ignores the horizontal-only momentum conservation reveals confusion between elastic/inelastic processes and the vector nature of momentum.

questions.q: A student argues: "When a bomb at rest explodes into two pieces, the pieces fly in opposite directions with equal speeds because momentum is conserved." Evaluate this statement and correct it if necessary.
questions.a: The statement is **false**. Momentum conservation gives \( m_1 \vec{v}_1 + m_2 \vec{v}_2 = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{v}_2 = -\frac{m_1}{m_2} \vec{v}_1 \). Speeds are equal **only if masses are equal** (\( m_1 = m_2 \)). For unequal masses, the lighter piece has greater speed. A student who agrees has oversimplified momentum conservation to "equal and opposite speeds" instead of "equal and opposite momenta".

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a low-friction trolley, a ball, and a spring-loaded launcher to demonstrate that the centre of mass of the (trolley + ball) system moves with constant velocity when the ball is launched internally. Describe the measurements needed.
questions.a: Place a ball in a spring launcher fixed on a trolley on a smooth horizontal track. Release the spring so the ball shoots forward and the trolley recoils backward. Use a smartphone camera to record the motion. Track positions of trolley centre and ball frame-by-frame. Compute \( x_{cm} = \frac{m_{trolley} x_{trolley} + m_{ball} x_{ball}}{M} \) for each frame. Plot \( x_{cm} \) vs time; it should be a straight line (constant velocity). A poor design would omit mass measurements, use a rough surface (external friction), or fail to track both objects simultaneously.
